title: Knee Osteoarthritis
case: Case: A 63-year-old teacher has 18 months of bilateral knee pain, worse on stairs and after walking, with 15 minutes of morning stiffness. Her right knee has crepitus, mild effusion and reduced flexion. She is overweight and avoids walking. Hip examination is normal. No fever, no calf swelling, no injury.

Working diagnosis: bilateral knee osteoarthritis. Plan: education, a regular strengthening and walking program, weight support, a stick on the left in the right hand, footwear review, measure chair stand and TUG, reassess every 4 to 6 weeks.

differentials.name: Patellofemoral pain

differentials.name: Meniscal tear
differentials.key: Locking, catching, joint-line pain, effusion after twisting

differentials.name: Hip osteoarthritis
differentials.key: Groin pain, limited hip rotation, pain referred to knee

differentials.name: Inflammatory arthritis
differentials.key: Morning stiffness over 30 minutes, several joints, swelling

differentials.name: Gout or pseudogout
differentials.key: Sudden hot, red, very painful joint

differentials.name: Septic arthritis
differentials.key: Hot, swollen joint, fever, unable to move

differentials.name: Osteonecrosis

qa: Why is X-ray not required for diagnosis here? The age, pain pattern and short stiffness are enough for a clinical diagnosis in most guidelines, and X-ray findings do not always match symptoms [Ref - to verify].
Why is exercise a core treatment even when the knee hurts? It improves pain, strength and function in many people, and avoiding movement tends to worsen weakness and stiffness [Ref - to verify].
The knee suddenly becomes hot and swollen and the patient has a fever. What do you do? Stop, refer to hospital the same day for possible joint infection.
Why not promise that the knee will be cured? OA is long-term, but symptoms can improve and be controlled with regular activity and self-management.
Why test chair stand and TUG? They measure real-life function and provide a baseline to track progress.

fields.Position and action: Supine, knee extended; stroke fluid up the inner side of the knee, then stroke down the outer side
fields.Positive: A bulge appears on the inner side

fields.Position and action: Supine, knee extended; push fluid out of the suprapatellar pouch with one hand, tap the patella down with the other hand
fields.Positive: The patella floats and taps against the femur

redFlags.Finding: Hot, red, swollen knee with fever or unable to move the joint
redFlags.Immediate action: Same-day hospital; do not exercise or mobilise

redFlags.Finding: Sudden hot swollen painful joint, no fever
redFlags.Urgency: Urgent same day or next day

redFlags.Finding: Injury with inability to take weight, bony tenderness, or inability to bend to 90 degrees, age 55 or older
redFlags.Immediate action: Use local injury decision rule (such as the Ottawa knee rules) and refer for imaging [Ref - to verify]

redFlags.Finding: Calf swelling, warmth, pain, or sudden breathlessness
Sudden severe pain at rest in an older person, night pain
Weight loss, constant night pain, cancer history

manual.name: Knee joint mobilization
manual.why: May give short-term pain relief and movement gains [Ref - to verify]
manual.application: Supine or sitting, gentle tibiofemoral and patellar glides, low to moderate grade

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and exercise. Manual therapy is optional as a short-term adjunct, usually combined with exercise. Do not claim that it restores cartilage or reverses the arthritis. Evidence for manual therapy alone is low in certainty [Ref - to verify].

exercise.Steps: Stand up from a chair and sit slowly
exercise.Regress when: Pain above about 4 out of 10 that lasts into the next day

exercise.Exercise: Straight leg raise or seated knee extension
exercise.Steps: Lift the leg with a light weight if needed
Use a rail, step up and control the step down
Lying on the side, lift the top leg

exercise.Starting dose: 10 to 20 minutes, 3 to 5 days a week

exercise.Exercise: Range exercise (heel slides, knee extension holds)

exerciseNotes: Principle: exercise is a first-line treatment for knee OA in nearly all major guidelines [Ref - to verify]. A common approach combines strengthening with aerobic activity, two to three times a week, supervised or as a home program. The type of exercise matters less than doing it regularly, progressing it gradually and continuing it.

Symptom rule: pain during exercise up to about 4 out of 10 that settles within about 24 hours is generally acceptable [Ref - to verify]. Pain that rises sharply, a hot swollen knee, or new instability means reduce load and reassess.
Weight management: if the patient is overweight, even modest weight loss can reduce pain [Ref - to verify]. Discuss respectfully, using the patient's goals, and refer to a dietitian when available.

Aids: a walking stick held in the hand opposite the painful knee may reduce load. Supportive, cushioned footwear is advised. Routine use of lateral wedge insoles is not recommended in several guidelines [Ref - to verify]. Knee braces may help selected patients.

modalities.name: Heat or cold
modalities.comment: Short-term comfort before or after exercise

modalities.name: TENS
modalities.comment: Short-term pain relief; limited long-term benefit [Ref - to verify]

modalities.name: Taping (e.g. patellar taping)
modalities.comment: May reduce pain in some patients; limited evidence

modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): topical anti-inflammatory gels, oral medication, corticosteroid injection for short-term relief of flares, and total or partial knee replacement for severe cases [Ref - to verify]. Rehabilitation before and after surgery improves readiness and recovery, and follows the surgeon's protocol.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Age 45 or over, activity-related knee pain, short or no morning stiffness? Yes: working diagnosis is knee OA (routine imaging is not needed).
Findings suggest another cause (locking, long morning stiffness, injury, hip pain)? Use that pathway.
Start core treatments: education, exercise and weight management when relevant.
If symptoms remain severe and function is poor despite good non-surgical care, discuss specialist review for injections or joint replacement [Ref - to verify].
Visit 1: screen flags, confirm the clinical diagnosis, explain OA in plain language, and set a goal.
Early: reduce painful loading, start gentle range and strengthening, add aerobic activity.
Middle: progress strength and function; address weight, footwear and aids.
